newsitem.title: USA: U.S. declines to rule out Iraq strikes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. declines to rule out Iraq strikes.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Monday the United States sought no confrontation with Iraq, but he declined to rule out air strikes against the Gulf state and his top military adviser said, "We are not standing down."

"We have sought no confrontation with (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein," Clinton replied when asked if Iraq's decision to stop firing at allied jets policing Iraqi no-fly zones meant Washington could forego any immediate air strikes.

As the Pentagon continued a rapid military build-up in the Gulf, Clinton said he wanted to answer carefully in light of tensions raised by the continuing possibility of strikes against Iraqi targets. He avoided a conclusive statement on whether the likelihood was diminishing.
"My concern is that we limit Saddam Hussein's ability to threaten his neighbours, that we do it with the no-fly zone and that we keep our pilots safe," he told White House reporters.

At the Pentagon, Army General John Shalikashvili said U.S. intelligence was still getting "mixed" signals on Iraq's air defence movements in the south and Washington would continue its build-up, including plans to send 3,000 or more troops to Kuwait from Fort Hood, Texas.
"We are not standing down," said Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. "Whether air strikes will be necessary or not will very much depend Saddam Hussein's actions, not his words."
But in its Tuesday editions, the Washington Post quoted Pentagon officials as saying that the administration was reconsidering whether to send the additional U.S. troops to Kuwait.
"There is no firm decision yet on whether or not there's a need to send American troops into Kuwait," one official told the paper.

The United States has sent eight radar-evading F-117A stealth fighters to Kuwait and is moving the aircraft carrier Enterprise to the Gulf to join the carrier Carl Vinson on station there. They carry a total of more than 150 warplanes.

Washington began building up forces in the region for possible retaliatory strikes last week after Saddam's air defences repeatedly challenged allied planes patrolling no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq.
But allied support for such retaliation was tepid at best and it declined further after Saddam's government annouunced on Friday that it was stopping its challenges.
"The intelligence on the ground yesterday and continues to be today mixed," Shalikashvili told reporters.
"We see some (Iraqi air defence missile) sites returning back to garrison. We see others still out in field locations moving around as if they were trying to evade us," he said.
Clinton sent Defence Secretary William Perry on a swift tour of Gulf allied states over the weekend in a bid to shore up support for any U.S. strike against Iraq.

Both Saudi Arabia and Turkey have refused to allow U.S. warplanes based on their territory to attack Iraq, even though they were part of the coalition that drove Iraqi occupying forces out of Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.
There was no indication Perry had changed minds in Riyadh or Ankara.

But Pentagon officials said after Perry visited Bahrain over the weekend that the small Gulf emirate had agreed to base more than 20 F-16 fighter jets on its territory to help patrol an expanded no-fly zone over southern Iraq.

In addition to those warplanes, the United States last week moved four B-52 bombers armed with cruise missiles to a British air base on the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia where they could take part in any new strikes on Iraq.
U.S. warships in the gulf and B-52s based on Guam fired missiles at air defences defences in southern Iraq on Sept. 3-4 in retaliation for attacks by Saddam's forces against Kurds in northern Iraq.
The United States later warned Saddam in both a diplomatic note and in statements from Perry and Shalikashvili not to "reconstitute" its air damaged air defences.
